Generalized OT Problems

The second family changes the optimization problem rather than only the ground distance. Barycenters average several measures, multi-marginal OT couples many measures at once, inverse OT learns the cost from observed transport, and weak OT allows randomized conditional responses.

These formulations remain close to Kantorovich linear programming, but the object being optimized is richer than a single two-marginal coupling.

Guiding Comparison

Barycenters optimize over the unknown measure being averaged. Multi-marginal OT optimizes over a whole joint law with several marginals. Inverse OT makes the ground cost the unknown. Weak OT keeps the marginal constraints but lets the cost depend on conditional laws rather than only on pointwise pairs.

OT Barycenters¶

Barycenters ask how to average probability measures rather than points. This section explains the variational definition, the special closed forms in one dimension and for Gaussians, and the entropic algorithms used in practice.

Frechet Means¶

For discrete input histograms {bs}s=1S\{b_s\}_{s=1}^S{bs​}s=1S​, with bs∈Δnsb_s\in\simplex_{n_s}bs​∈Δns​​, and weights λ∈ΔS\lambda\in\simplex_Sλ∈ΔS​, a Wasserstein barycenter can be computed by minimizing

min⁡a∈Δn∑s=1Sλs LCs(a,bs),\min_{a\in\simplex_n} \sum_{s=1}^S \lambda_s\,\mathcal L_{C_s}(a,b_s),a∈Δn​min​s=1∑S​λs​LCs​​(a,bs​),
(1)

where the cost matrices Cs∈Rn×nsC_s\in\RR^{n\times n_s}Cs​∈Rn×ns​ are prescribed. This barycenter problem was introduced by Carlier and coauthors, following earlier matching ideas, and is the measure-valued analogue of a Frechet mean Agueh & Carlier, 2011Carlier & Ekeland, 2010.

Given input measures (βs)s(\beta_s)_s(βs​)s​ on a space X\XX, the barycenter problem is

min⁡α∈M+1(X)∑s=1Sλs Lc(α,βs).\min_{\alpha\in\mathcal M_+^1(\X)} \sum_{s=1}^S \lambda_s\,\mathcal L_c(\alpha,\beta_s).α∈M+1​(X)min​s=1∑S​λs​Lc​(α,βs​).
(2)

For X=Rd\X=\RR^dX=Rd and c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2c(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^2c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2, if one input measure has a density, then the barycenter is unique Agueh & Carlier, 2011. Discrete existence, consistency, and fixed-point constructions are studied in Anderes et al., 2016Esteban et al., 2016Le Gouic & Loubes, 2016.

Example: Two measures recover a Wasserstein geodesic

For S=2S=2S=2, c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2c(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^2c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2 and weights (1−t,t)(1-t,t)(1−t,t), the barycenter is the point at time ttt on the Wasserstein geodesic between β0\beta_0β0​ and β1\beta_1β1​. If TTT is the Brenier map from β0\beta_0β0​ to β1\beta_1β1​, this barycenter is ((1−t)Id+tT)♯β0((1-t)\Id+tT)_\sharp\beta_0((1−t)Id+tT)♯​β0​, the McCann interpolation detailed in Section Geodesic Convexity and Convergence. If no Monge map is available, the same construction uses an optimal coupling π\piπ and the interpolation map (x,y)↦(1−t)x+ty(x,y)\mapsto(1-t)x+ty(x,y)↦(1−t)x+ty, giving ((1−t)x+ty)♯π((1-t)x+ty)_\sharp\pi((1−t)x+ty)♯​π.

Example: Dirac inputs recover Fr'echet means

Problem (2) generalizes the computation of barycenters of points (xs)s=1S∈XS(x_s)_{s=1}^S \in \X^S(xs​)s=1S​∈XS to arbitrary measures. Indeed, if βs=δxs\be_s=\de_{x_s}βs​=δxs​​ is a single Dirac mass, then a solution to (2) is δx⋆\de_{x^\star}δx⋆​ where x⋆x^\starx⋆ is a Frechet mean of the points (xs)s(x_s)_s(xs​)s​.

Remark: Mean of a quadratic barycenter

For c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2c(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^2c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2, the mean of the barycenter α⋆\al^\starα⋆ is necessarily the barycenter of the means,

∫Xx dα⋆(x)=∑sλs∫Xx dβs(x).\int_\Xx x \d\al^\star(x) = \sum_s \la_s \int_\Xx x \d\be_s(x).∫X​xdα⋆(x)=s∑​λs​∫X​xdβs​(x).
(3)

Indeed, the squared Wasserstein distance decomposes into a squared distance between means plus a centered Wasserstein term. Minimizing the resulting quadratic function of the barycenter mean gives the displayed identity. If the input measures have compact support, the usual multi-marginal barycentric construction also gives a barycenter supported in the convex hull of the input supports.

Proposition: Convexity of the OT Cost

The map (α,β)↦Lc(α,β)(\alpha,\beta)\mapsto\mathcal L_c(\alpha,\beta)(α,β)↦Lc​(α,β) is convex.

Proof

Let (α0,β0)(\alpha_0,\beta_0)(α0​,β0​) and (α1,β1)(\alpha_1,\beta_1)(α1​,β1​) be two pairs of probability measures and let t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]t∈[0,1]. For η>0\eta>0η>0, choose couplings πi∈Π(αi,βi)\pi_i\in\Couplings(\alpha_i,\beta_i)πi​∈Π(αi​,βi​) such that

∫c dπi≤Lc(αi,βi)+η(i=0,1).\int c\d\pi_i \leq \mathcal L_c(\alpha_i,\beta_i)+\eta \qquad (i=0,1).∫cdπi​≤Lc​(αi​,βi​)+η(i=0,1).
(4)

Then πt=(1−t)π0+tπ1\pi_t=(1-t)\pi_0+t\pi_1πt​=(1−t)π0​+tπ1​ is a coupling between (1−t)α0+tα1(1-t)\alpha_0+t\alpha_1(1−t)α0​+tα1​ and (1−t)β0+tβ1(1-t)\beta_0+t\beta_1(1−t)β0​+tβ1​. Hence

Lc((1−t)α0+tα1,(1−t)β0+tβ1)≤(1−t)Lc(α0,β0)+tLc(α1,β1)+η.\mathcal L_c((1-t)\alpha_0+t\alpha_1,(1-t)\beta_0+t\beta_1) \leq (1-t)\mathcal L_c(\alpha_0,\beta_0) + t\mathcal L_c(\alpha_1,\beta_1) + \eta .Lc​((1−t)α0​+tα1​,(1−t)β0​+tβ1​)≤(1−t)Lc​(α0​,β0​)+tLc​(α1​,β1​)+η.
(5)

Letting η→0\eta\to0η→0 gives the claim.

Even when all input measures are discrete, the support of a barycenter is not known a priori. The multi-marginal formulation below shows that a discrete barycenter can be supported on all weighted averages of one support point from each input. This gives at most ∏sns\prod_s n_s∏s​ns​ candidate points if the sss-th input has nsn_sns​ atoms, which is prohibitive when the number of inputs is large. A common numerical compromise is therefore to prescribe a smaller support for the barycenter and solve a fixed-support problem.

One-Dimensional Case¶

On the line, barycenters become linear after the quantile change of variables. This gives the rare case where the barycenter is explicit rather than the solution of a high-dimensional optimization problem.

Proposition: Quantile Barycenters on the Line

For X=R\X=\RRX=R and c(x,y)=∣x−y∣2c(x,y)=|x-y|^2c(x,y)=∣x−y∣2, the quantile function of a Wasserstein barycenter is the weighted average of the input quantile functions:

Fα⋆−1(r)=∑s=1SλsFβs−1(r),r∈[0,1].F_{\alpha^\star}^{-1}(r) = \sum_{s=1}^S \lambda_s F_{\beta_s}^{-1}(r), \qquad r\in[0,1].Fα⋆−1​(r)=s=1∑S​λs​Fβs​−1​(r),r∈[0,1].
(6)
Proof

The one-dimensional formula for W2\Wass_2W2​ gives

∑sλsW22(α,βs)=∫01∑sλs∣Fα−1(r)−Fβs−1(r)∣2 dr.\sum_s\lambda_s\Wass_2^2(\alpha,\beta_s) = \int_0^1 \sum_s\lambda_s \abs{F_\alpha^{-1}(r)-F_{\beta_s}^{-1}(r)}^2 \d r.s∑​λs​W22​(α,βs​)=∫01​s∑​λs​∣∣​Fα−1​(r)−Fβs​−1​(r)∣∣​2dr.
(7)

The minimization decouples pointwise in rrr. For each fixed rrr, the minimizer of z↦∑sλs∣z−Fβs−1(r)∣2z\mapsto\sum_s\lambda_s|z-F_{\beta_s}^{-1}(r)|^2z↦∑s​λs​∣z−Fβs​−1​(r)∣2 is the weighted average ∑sλsFβs−1(r)\sum_s\lambda_sF_{\beta_s}^{-1}(r)∑s​λs​Fβs​−1​(r). This function is nondecreasing because it is a positive weighted sum of nondecreasing quantile functions, hence it is a valid quantile function.

Gaussian Case¶

Gaussian barycenters show that the same separation as in the Gaussian Wasserstein formula persists: means average linearly, while covariances average according to the Bures--Wasserstein geometry.

Example: Gaussian inputs remain Gaussian

The barycenter of Gaussian measures is Gaussian. In one dimension, it is obtained by averaging the means and the standard deviations, so the barycenter variance is the square of this averaged standard deviation. In higher dimensions, the covariance Σ\covΣ minimizes the Bures objective

Σ↦∑sλsB(Σ,Σs)2,\cov \mapsto \sum_s \la_s \Bb(\cov,\cov_s)^2,Σ↦s∑​λs​B(Σ,Σs​)2,
(8)

and equivalently solves the fixed-point equation

Σ=∑sλs(Σ1/2ΣsΣ1/2)1/2.\cov = \sum_s \la_s \pa{\cov^{1/2}\cov_s\cov^{1/2}}^{1/2}.Σ=s∑​λs​(Σ1/2Σs​Σ1/2)1/2.
(9)

This is the covariance analogue of the usual Euclidean barycenter equation: the mean part averages linearly, while the covariance part averages through the Bures--Wasserstein geometry Esteban et al., 2016Bhatia et al., 2019.

Sinkhorn for Barycenters¶

A key difference with the regularized two-marginal OT problem is that there is no canonical reference measure α⊗β\alpha\otimes\betaα⊗β, because the barycenter α\alphaα is unknown. To reduce complexity, one usually fixes a candidate support for the barycenter and solves the discrete problem (1); this introduces a discretization error but keeps the number of unknowns manageable.

One can then use entropic smoothing and approximate (1) by

min⁡a∈Δn∑s=1SλsLCsϵ(a,bs)\min_{a\in\simplex_n} \sum_{s=1}^S \lambda_s\mathcal L_{C_s}^{\epsilon}(a,b_s)a∈Δn​min​s=1∑S​λs​LCs​ϵ​(a,bs​)
(10)

for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0. This is a smooth convex minimization problem, which can be tackled using gradient descent Cuturi & Doucet, 2014. An alternative is to use a descent method, typically quasi-Newton, on the semi-dual Cuturi & Peyré, 2016; this is useful when adding extra regularization on the barycenter, for instance to impose smoothness.

A simple but effective approach rewrites (10) as a weighted KL projection problem Benamou et al., 2015:

min⁡(Ps)sϵ∑sλsKL⁡(Ps∣Ks)\min_{(P_s)_s} \epsilon\sum_s\lambda_s \operatorname{KL}(P_s\mid K_s)(Ps​)s​min​ϵs∑​λs​KL(Ps​∣Ks​)
(11)

subject to

Ps⊤1n=bsfor all s,P11n1=⋯=PS1nS.P_s^\top\mathbf 1_n=b_s \quad\text{for all }s, \qquad P_1\mathbf 1_{n_1} = \cdots = P_S\mathbf 1_{n_S}.Ps⊤​1n​=bs​for all s,P1​1n1​​=⋯=PS​1nS​​.
(12)

Here Ks:=e−Cs/ϵK_s\eqdef e^{-C_s/\epsilon}Ks​:=e−Cs​/ϵ. The barycenter aaa is implicitly encoded in the common row marginal

a=P11n1=⋯=PS1nS.a=P_1\mathbf 1_{n_1}=\cdots=P_S\mathbf 1_{n_S}.a=P1​1n1​​=⋯=PS​1nS​​.
(13)

The optimal couplings have scaling form

Ps=diag⁡(us)Ksdiag⁡(vs),P_s=\diag(u_s)K_s\diag(v_s),Ps​=diag(us​)Ks​diag(vs​),
(14)

and the generalized Sinkhorn iterations are

vs←bsKs⊤us,a←∏s(Ksvs)λs,us←aKsvs.v_s\leftarrow\frac{b_s}{K_s^\top u_s}, \qquad a\leftarrow\prod_s(K_s v_s)^{\lambda_s}, \qquad u_s\leftarrow\frac{a}{K_s v_s}.vs​←Ks⊤​us​bs​​,a←s∏​(Ks​vs​)λs​,us​←Ks​vs​a​.
(15)

The geometric mean enforces the fact that all couplings share the same barycenter marginal.

Proposition: Dual of Entropic Barycenters

The optimal scalings in (14) can be written as (us,vs)=(efs/ϵ,egs/ϵ)(u_s,v_s)=(e^{f_s/\epsilon},e^{g_s/\epsilon})(us​,vs​)=(efs​/ϵ,egs​/ϵ), where (fs,gs)s(f_s,g_s)_s(fs​,gs​)s​ solve

max⁡(fs,gs)s∑sλs(⟨gs,bs⟩−ϵ⟨Ksegs/ϵ,efs/ϵ⟩)subject to∑sλsfs=0.\max_{(f_s,g_s)_s} \sum_s\lambda_s \left( \dotp{g_s}{b_s} - \epsilon\dotp{K_s e^{g_s/\epsilon}}{e^{f_s/\epsilon}} \right) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_s\lambda_s f_s=0.(fs​,gs​)s​max​s∑​λs​(⟨gs​,bs​⟩−ϵ⟨Ks​egs​/ϵ,efs​/ϵ⟩)subject tos∑​λs​fs​=0.
(16)
Proof

Introduce Lagrange multipliers in (11):

min⁡(Ps)s,amax⁡(fs,gs)s∑sλs(ϵKL⁡(Ps∣Ks)+⟨a−Ps1ns,fs⟩+⟨bs−Ps⊤1n,gs⟩).\min_{(P_s)_s,a} \max_{(f_s,g_s)_s} \sum_s\lambda_s \left( \epsilon\operatorname{KL}(P_s\mid K_s) + \dotp{a-P_s\mathbf 1_{n_s}}{f_s} + \dotp{b_s-P_s^\top\mathbf 1_n}{g_s} \right).(Ps​)s​,amin​(fs​,gs​)s​max​s∑​λs​(ϵKL(Ps​∣Ks​)+⟨a−Ps​1ns​​,fs​⟩+⟨bs​−Ps⊤​1n​,gs​⟩).
(17)

Strong duality allows one to exchange the minimum and maximum. Minimizing with respect to aaa gives the constraint ∑sλsfs=0\sum_s\lambda_s f_s=0∑s​λs​fs​=0, and minimizing with respect to PsP_sPs​ gives the Legendre transform of KL⁡(⋅∣Ks)\operatorname{KL}(\cdot\mid K_s)KL(⋅∣Ks​):

max⁡(fs,gs)s∑sλs[⟨gs,bs⟩−ϵKL⁡∗(fs⊕gsϵ|Ks)],∑sλsfs=0.\max_{(f_s,g_s)_s} \sum_s\lambda_s \left[ \dotp{g_s}{b_s} - \epsilon \operatorname{KL}^* \left(\frac{f_s\oplus g_s}{\epsilon}\middle|K_s\right) \right], \qquad \sum_s\lambda_s f_s=0.(fs​,gs​)s​max​s∑​λs​[⟨gs​,bs​⟩−ϵKL∗(ϵfs​⊕gs​​∣∣​Ks​)],s∑​λs​fs​=0.

The separable conjugate is

KL⁡∗(U∣K)=∑i,jKi,j(eUi,j−1),\operatorname{KL}^*(U\mid K) = \sum_{i,j}K_{i,j}(e^{U_{i,j}}-1),KL∗(U∣K)=i,j∑​Ki,j​(eUi,j​−1),
(19)

because for k>0k>0k>0,

sup⁡r≥0ur−(rlog⁡(r/k)−r+k)=k(eu−1).\sup_{r\geq0} ur-\big(r\log(r/k)-r+k\big) = k(e^u-1).r≥0sup​ur−(rlog(r/k)−r+k)=k(eu−1).
(20)

Dropping constants independent of the potentials gives the displayed dual. Coordinate maximization in gsg_sgs​ gives the vsv_svs​ update; block maximization in all (fs)s(f_s)_s(fs​)s​ gives the common marginal update and then the usu_sus​ update.

Classical applications include two-dimensional image interpolation, three-dimensional shape interpolation, and barycenters on surfaces where the ground cost is the square of the geodesic distance Solomon et al., 2015.

Multimarginal OT¶

Multi-marginal OT couples more than two measures at once. It is the natural language for barycenters, matching with teams and several-body costs, but its tensor dimension is the main computational obstacle.

Definition and Basic Structure¶

The multi-marginal formulation replaces a coupling between two measures by a joint distribution with several prescribed marginals. Given measures (αs)s=1S(\alpha_s)_{s=1}^S(αs​)s=1S​ on spaces (Xs)s=1S(\X_s)_{s=1}^S(Xs​)s=1S​ and a cost c:X1×⋯×XS→Rc:\X_1\times\cdots\times\X_S\to\RRc:X1​×⋯×XS​→R, the problem reads

inf⁡π∈Π(α1,…,αS)∫X1×⋯×XSc(x1,…,xS) dπ(x1,…,xS),\inf_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_S)} \int_{\X_1\times\cdots\times\X_S} c(x_1,\ldots,x_S)\d\pi(x_1,\ldots,x_S),π∈Π(α1​,…,αS​)inf​∫X1​×⋯×XS​​c(x1​,…,xS​)dπ(x1​,…,xS​),
(21)

where Π(α1,…,αS)\Couplings(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_S)Π(α1​,…,αS​) is the set of probability measures whose sss-th marginal is αs\alpha_sαs​. This is still a linear program in the discrete setting, but its ambient tensor has size ∏sns\prod_s n_s∏s​ns​.

Monge Structure and Splitting-Set Twist¶

As in the two-marginal case, one would like to know when the optimal joint law is induced by deterministic maps from one marginal. The relevant non-degeneracy assumption is stronger than pairwise twist, because the other S−1S-1S−1 variables have to be recovered simultaneously. The condition below is the standard multi-marginal analogue used in the Monge-structure theory of Gangbo--Swiech and Pass Gangbo & Swiech, 1998Pass, 2011Pass, 2012Pass, 2015.

Definition: Twist on Splitting Sets

Fix x1∈X1x_1\in\X_1x1​∈X1​. A set M⊂X2×⋯×XSM\subset\X_2\times\cdots\times\X_SM⊂X2​×⋯×XS​ is a ccc-splitting set at x1x_1x1​ if there exist functions us:Xs→R∪{−∞}u_s:\X_s\to\RR\cup\{-\infty\}us​:Xs​→R∪{−∞}, for s=2,…,Ss=2,\ldots,Ss=2,…,S, such that

∑s=2Sus(xs)≤c(x1,x2,…,xS)\sum_{s=2}^S u_s(x_s)\leq c(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_S)s=2∑S​us​(xs​)≤c(x1​,x2​,…,xS​)
(22)

for all (x2,…,xS)(x_2,\ldots,x_S)(x2​,…,xS​), with equality on MMM. Assume ccc is differentiable in x1x_1x1​. The cost is twisted on splitting sets if, for every x1x_1x1​ and every ccc-splitting set MMM at x1x_1x1​, the map

(x2,…,xS)⟼∇x1c(x1,x2,…,xS)(x_2,\ldots,x_S) \longmapsto \nabla_{x_1}c(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_S)(x2​,…,xS​)⟼∇x1​​c(x1​,x2​,…,xS​)
(23)

is injective on MMM.

Proposition: Multi-Marginal Monge Structure

Assume that Xs⊂Rd\X_s\subset\RR^dXs​⊂Rd, that ccc is continuous and differentiable with respect to x1x_1x1​, and that ccc is twisted on splitting sets. Suppose that Kantorovich dual maximizers (φs)s=1S(\varphi_s)_{s=1}^S(φs​)s=1S​ exist and that φ1\varphi_1φ1​ is differentiable α1\alpha_1α1​-a.e. If α1\alpha_1α1​ is absolutely continuous, then every optimal plan π⋆∈Π(α1,…,αS)\pi^\star\in\Couplings(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_S)π⋆∈Π(α1​,…,αS​) is concentrated on the graph of maps

π⋆=(Id,T2,…,TS)♯α1,(Ts)♯α1=αs.\pi^\star=(\Id,\T_2,\ldots,\T_S)_\sharp\alpha_1, \qquad (\T_s)_\sharp\alpha_1=\alpha_s.π⋆=(Id,T2​,…,TS​)♯​α1​,(Ts​)♯​α1​=αs​.
(24)

In particular, under these hypotheses the optimizer is unique.

Proof

Let (φs)s=1S(\varphi_s)_{s=1}^S(φs​)s=1S​ be optimal dual potentials, so that ∑sφs(xs)≤c(x1,…,xS)\sum_s\varphi_s(x_s)\leq c(x_1,\ldots,x_S)∑s​φs​(xs​)≤c(x1​,…,xS​) with equality on supp⁡(π⋆)\operatorname{supp}(\pi^\star)supp(π⋆). Fix a point x1x_1x1​ where φ1\varphi_1φ1​ is differentiable and consider the fiber

M(x1)={(x2,…,xS):(x1,x2,…,xS)∈supp⁡(π⋆)}.M(x_1) = \{(x_2,\ldots,x_S):(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_S)\in\operatorname{supp}(\pi^\star)\}.M(x1​)={(x2​,…,xS​):(x1​,x2​,…,xS​)∈supp(π⋆)}.
(25)

Equivalently, set u2=φ2+φ1(x1)u_2=\varphi_2+\varphi_1(x_1)u2​=φ2​+φ1​(x1​) and us=φsu_s=\varphi_sus​=φs​ for s≥3s\geq3s≥3. Dual feasibility gives ∑s=2Sus(xs)≤c(x1,x2,…,xS)\sum_{s=2}^S u_s(x_s)\leq c(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_S)∑s=2S​us​(xs​)≤c(x1​,x2​,…,xS​), with equality on M(x1)M(x_1)M(x1​). ∇φ1(x1)=∇x1c(x1,x2,…,xS).\nabla\varphi_1(x_1)=\nabla_{x_1}c(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_S).∇φ1​(x1​)=∇x1​​c(x1​,x2​,…,xS​).
(27)

All points in the fiber therefore have the same value of ∇x1c\nabla_{x_1}c∇x1​​c. Twist on splitting sets makes the fiber a singleton for α1\alpha_1α1​-a.e. x1x_1x1​. Disintegrating π⋆\pi^\starπ⋆ with respect to its first marginal gives Dirac conditional measures, hence measurable maps (T2,…,TS)(\T_2,\ldots,\T_S)(T2​,…,TS​). If π1\pi^1π1 and π2\pi^2π2 are two optimal plans, their average is also optimal. The conditional measure of this average over x1x_1x1​ is the average of the two Dirac conditionals, and it must again be a Dirac mass by the preceding argument. Hence the two Dirac masses coincide for α1\alpha_1α1​-a.e. x1x_1x1​, proving uniqueness.

Coulomb Cost and Density-Functional Theory¶

A second canonical example, besides barycenters, comes from electronic structure. For NNN electrons in R3\RR^3R3, the repulsive Coulomb interaction is the multi-body cost

cCoul(x1,…,xN):=∑1≤i<j≤N1∥xi−xj∥,c_{\mathrm{Coul}}(x_1,\ldots,x_N) \eqdef \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\frac{1}{\norm{x_i-x_j}},cCoul​(x1​,…,xN​):=1≤i<j≤N∑​∥xi​−xj​∥1​,
(28)

with the value +∞+\infty+∞ on the collision set. This lower-semicontinuous singularity is not a harmless detail: finite-energy plans avoid electron collisions, and the smooth structure theorem above should be read as a guide rather than as a global theorem for the Coulomb cost. If ρ\rhoρ is an electron density with ∫R3ρ(x) dx=N\int_{\RR^3}\rho(x)\d x=N∫R3​ρ(x)dx=N and μ=ρ/N\mu=\rho/Nμ=ρ/N is the associated probability density, the strictly-correlated-electrons relaxation of density-functional theory is the equal-marginal problem

VeeSCE[ρ]:=inf⁡π∈Π(μ,…,μ)∫(R3)NcCoul(x1,…,xN) dπ(x1,…,xN).V_{\mathrm{ee}}^{\mathrm{SCE}}[\rho] \eqdef \inf_{\pi\in\Couplings(\mu,\ldots,\mu)} \int_{(\RR^3)^N} c_{\mathrm{Coul}}(x_1,\ldots,x_N) \d\pi(x_1,\ldots,x_N).VeeSCE​[ρ]:=π∈Π(μ,…,μ)inf​∫(R3)N​cCoul​(x1​,…,xN​)dπ(x1​,…,xN​).
(29)

Since the cost and constraints are permutation invariant, symmetrizing any admissible plan does not change its value, so one may equivalently minimize over symmetric plans. This functional gives the smallest possible electron--electron repulsion compatible with the prescribed one-particle density; it appears as the strong-interaction limit in density-functional theory and was connected to optimal transport in Gori-Giorgi et al., 2009Buttazzo et al., 2012Cotar et al., 2013Di Marino et al., 2015. The deterministic ansatz writes a plan through co-motion maps

π=(Id,T2,…,TN)♯μ,(Ti)♯μ=μ,\pi=(\Id,\T_2,\ldots,\T_N)_\sharp\mu, \qquad (\T_i)_\sharp\mu=\mu,π=(Id,T2​,…,TN​)♯​μ,(Ti​)♯​μ=μ,
(30)

so that the position of one electron determines the positions of the others. The following cyclic version is the most common structural form of this ansatz in the strictly-correlated-electrons literature.

Proposition: Cyclic Co-Motion Plans

Let μ∈P(R3)\mu\in\Pp(\RR^3)μ∈P(R3) and let T:R3→R3\T:\RR^3\to\RR^3T:R3→R3 be measurable with T♯μ=μ\T_\sharp\mu=\muT♯​μ=μ and TN=Id\T^N=\IdTN=Id μ\muμ-a.e. Set T0=Id\T^0=\IdT0=Id and

πT=(T0,T1,…,TN−1)♯μ.\pi_\T=(\T^0,\T^1,\ldots,\T^{N-1})_\sharp\mu .πT​=(T0,T1,…,TN−1)♯​μ.
(31)

Then πT∈Π(μ,…,μ)\pi_\T\in\Couplings(\mu,\ldots,\mu)πT​∈Π(μ,…,μ). If Rσ(x1,…,xN)=(xσ(1),…,xσ(N))R_\sigma(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=(x_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,x_{\sigma(N)})Rσ​(x1​,…,xN​)=(xσ(1)​,…,xσ(N)​) for σ∈Perm(N)\sigma\in\Perm(N)σ∈Perm(N), then

πˉT:=1N!∑σ∈Perm(N)(Rσ)♯πT\bar\pi_\T \eqdef \frac1{N!}\sum_{\sigma\in\Perm(N)}(R_\sigma)_\sharp\pi_\TπˉT​:=N!1​σ∈Perm(N)∑​(Rσ​)♯​πT​
(32)

is a symmetric admissible plan and

∫cCoul dπˉT=∫cCoul dπT=∫R3∑0≤i<j≤N−11∥Ti(x)−Tj(x)∥ dμ(x).\int c_{\mathrm{Coul}}\d\bar\pi_\T = \int c_{\mathrm{Coul}}\d\pi_\T = \int_{\RR^3} \sum_{0\leq i<j\leq N-1} \frac{1}{\norm{\T^i(x)-\T^j(x)}}\d\mu(x).∫cCoul​dπˉT​=∫cCoul​dπT​=∫R3​0≤i<j≤N−1∑​∥Ti(x)−Tj(x)∥1​dμ(x).
(33)
Proof

Since T♯μ=μ\T_\sharp\mu=\muT♯​μ=μ, all iterates Ti\T^iTi preserve μ\muμ, so every marginal of πT\pi_\TπT​ is μ\muμ. The plan πˉT\bar\pi_\TπˉT​ is an average of coordinate permutations of πT\pi_\TπT​, hence has the same marginals and is invariant under coordinate permutations. The Coulomb cost is symmetric in its arguments, so its integral is unchanged by each RσR_\sigmaRσ​. The last identity follows by evaluating cCoulc_{\mathrm{Coul}}cCoul​ on the graph (x,T(x),…,TN−1(x))(x,\T(x),\ldots,\T^{N-1}(x))(x,T(x),…,TN−1(x)).

The Monge-structure proposition above explains the general mechanism that can force graph solutions, while the cyclic co-motion proposition records the additional equal-marginal symmetry used by co-motion maps. For the Coulomb cost, however, the singular repulsion and permutation symmetry make the structure delicate: co-motion maps are optimal in special geometries, but they are not universally optimal, and counterexamples are known Colombo & Stra, 2015Bindini et al., 2020. Thus the DFT problem is both a central application and a warning that multi-marginal OT is richer than a naive deterministic matching problem.

Multi-Marginal Formulation of Barycenters¶

Wasserstein barycenters are the central example. For the squared Euclidean cost, one can introduce a latent barycenter point and eliminate it explicitly, leading to the multi-marginal cost

cbar(x1,…,xS)=min⁡x∈Rd∑s=1Sλs∥x−xs∥2.c_{\mathrm{bar}}(x_1,\ldots,x_S) = \min_{x\in\RR^d} \sum_{s=1}^S\lambda_s\norm{x-x_s}^2.cbar​(x1​,…,xS​)=x∈Rdmin​s=1∑S​λs​∥x−xs​∥2.
(34)
Proposition: Multi-Marginal Formula for Quadratic Barycenters

Let β1,…,βS∈P2(Rd)\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_S\in\mathcal P_2(\RR^d)β1​,…,βS​∈P2​(Rd) and λ∈ΔS\lambda\in\simplex_Sλ∈ΔS​. Define

B(x1,…,xS)=∑s=1Sλsxs,cbar(x1,…,xS)=min⁡x∑sλs∥x−xs∥2.B(x_1,\ldots,x_S)=\sum_{s=1}^S\lambda_s x_s, \qquad c_{\mathrm{bar}}(x_1,\ldots,x_S) = \min_x \sum_s\lambda_s\norm{x-x_s}^2.B(x1​,…,xS​)=s=1∑S​λs​xs​,cbar​(x1​,…,xS​)=xmin​s∑​λs​∥x−xs​∥2.
(35)

If π⋆\pi^\starπ⋆ solves the multi-marginal OT problem with marginals (βs)s(\beta_s)_s(βs​)s​ and cost cbarc_{\mathrm{bar}}cbar​, then α⋆=B♯π⋆\alpha^\star=B_\sharp\pi^\starα⋆=B♯​π⋆ is a Wasserstein barycenter. Conversely, every barycenter is obtained this way from an optimal multi-marginal plan.

Proof

For any candidate barycenter α\alphaα and couplings πs∈Π(α,βs)\pi_s\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta_s)πs​∈Π(α,βs​), glue the couplings along their common α\alphaα marginal to obtain a joint law of (X,Y1,…,YS)(X,Y_1,\ldots,Y_S)(X,Y1​,…,YS​). Conditioning on (Ys)s(Y_s)_s(Ys​)s​ and minimizing over XXX gives

∑sλsE∥X−Ys∥2≥Emin⁡x∑sλs∥x−Ys∥2=Ecbar(Y1,…,YS).\sum_s\lambda_s\mathbb E\norm{X-Y_s}^2 \geq \mathbb E \min_x \sum_s\lambda_s\norm{x-Y_s}^2 = \mathbb E c_{\mathrm{bar}}(Y_1,\ldots,Y_S).s∑​λs​E∥X−Ys​∥2≥Exmin​s∑​λs​∥x−Ys​∥2=Ecbar​(Y1​,…,YS​).
(36)

Taking the infimum over the couplings gives that the barycenter value is at least the multi-marginal value. Conversely, from an optimal multi-marginal plan π⋆\pi^\starπ⋆, set X=B(Y1,…,YS)X=B(Y_1,\ldots,Y_S)X=B(Y1​,…,YS​). The couplings between XXX and each YsY_sYs​ are feasible for the barycenter problem and attain exactly the multi-marginal cost.

If α⋆\alpha^\starα⋆ is any barycenter, choose optimal couplings between α⋆\alpha^\starα⋆ and each βs\beta_sβs​ and glue them along the common α⋆\alpha^\starα⋆ marginal. Since the barycenter and multi-marginal values are equal, the conditional minimization inequality above must be an equality. Thus X=B(Y1,…,YS)X=B(Y_1,\ldots,Y_S)X=B(Y1​,…,YS​) almost surely for the induced optimal multi-marginal plan.

Corollary: Gaussian and Discrete Barycenters

Quadratic Wasserstein barycenters of Gaussian measures are Gaussian. If the input measures are discrete, then there exists a barycenter supported on the set of weighted averages ∑sλsxs,is\sum_s\lambda_s x_{s,i_s}∑s​λs​xs,is​​ of one support point from each input. In particular, if the sss-th input has nsn_sns​ atoms, a barycenter exists with at most ∏sns\prod_s n_s∏s​ns​ atoms.

Proof

Let the input Gaussians have means msm_sms​ and covariances Σs\Sigma_sΣs​. For any candidate barycenter α\alphaα with mean mmm and covariance Σ\SigmaΣ, Gelbrich’s inequality gives

W22(α,βs)≥∥m−ms∥2+B(Σ,Σs)2,\Wass_2^2(\alpha,\beta_s) \geq \norm{m-m_s}^2+\mathcal B(\Sigma,\Sigma_s)^2,W22​(α,βs​)≥∥m−ms​∥2+B(Σ,Σs​)2,
(37)

with equality for the Gaussian law with mean mmm and covariance Σ\SigmaΣ. Therefore the barycenter objective is bounded below by a function depending only on (m,Σ)(m,\Sigma)(m,Σ), and this lower bound is attained by the Gaussian measure with the minimizing mean and covariance. For discrete inputs, any multi-marginal optimizer is supported on the finite product of the input supports, and BBB maps this product to at most ∏sns\prod_s n_s∏s​ns​ points.

Entropic Regularization of Multi-Marginal OT¶

As in the two-marginal case, adding an entropic penalty with respect to the product measure α1⊗⋯⊗αS\alpha_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\alpha_Sα1​⊗⋯⊗αS​ leads to scaling algorithms:

inf⁡π∈Π(α1,…,αS)∫c dπ+ϵKL⁡(π∣α1⊗⋯⊗αS).\inf_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_S)} \int c\d\pi + \epsilon\operatorname{KL} (\pi\mid\alpha_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\alpha_S).π∈Π(α1​,…,αS​)inf​∫cdπ+ϵKL(π∣α1​⊗⋯⊗αS​).
(38)

The optimizer has the generalized Gibbs form

 dπ⋆(x1,…,xS)=exp⁡ ⁣(∑sfs(xs)−c(x1,…,xS)ϵ)∏s dαs(xs),\d\pi^\star(x_1,\ldots,x_S) = \exp\!\left( \frac{\sum_s f_s(x_s)-c(x_1,\ldots,x_S)}{\epsilon} \right) \prod_s\d\alpha_s(x_s),dπ⋆(x1​,…,xS​)=exp(ϵ∑s​fs​(xs​)−c(x1​,…,xS​)​)s∏​dαs​(xs​),
(39)

and generalized Sinkhorn iterations alternately update one potential fsf_sfs​ so that the sss-th marginal is correct. The bottleneck is the tensor size ∏sns\prod_s n_s∏s​ns​ in the discrete case. Practical barycenter solvers exploit separability of the cost, low-rank structure, convolutional kernels, or a fixed barycenter support.

Low-Rank Optimal Transport¶

Low-rank OT reduces the size of a transport plan by forcing the coupling itself to pass through a small latent measure. This is useful when the mass exchange is expected to be organized by a few hidden clusters or prototypes, and it is distinct from approximating the Sinkhorn kernel by a low-rank matrix. The idea was introduced statistically through factored couplings by Forrow, Hütter, Nitzan, Rigollet, Schiebinger and Weed Forrow et al., 2019, and developed algorithmically for arbitrary costs by Scetbon, Cuturi and Peyré Scetbon et al., 2021.

Definition: Low-Rank Factored Couplings

Let a∈Δna\in\simplex_na∈Δn​, b∈Δmb\in\simplex_mb∈Δm​ and let r≥1r\geq1r≥1. A rank-rrr factored coupling is a triple (Q,R,g)(Q,R,g)(Q,R,g) such that

Q∈R+n×r,R∈R+m×r,g∈Δr,Q\in\RR_+^{n\times r},\qquad R\in\RR_+^{m\times r}, \qquad g\in\simplex_r,Q∈R+n×r​,R∈R+m×r​,g∈Δr​,
(40)

with

Q1r=a,R1r=b,Q⊤1n=R⊤1m=g.Q\ones_r=a, \qquad R\ones_r=b, \qquad Q^\top\ones_n=R^\top\ones_m=g.Q1r​=a,R1r​=b,Q⊤1n​=R⊤1m​=g.
(41)

It induces the coupling

P(Q,R,g)=Qdiag⁡(g)−1R⊤,Pi,j=∑k=1rQi,kRj,kgk,P(Q,R,g) = Q\operatorname{diag}(g)^{-1}R^\top, \qquad P_{i,j}=\sum_{k=1}^r \frac{Q_{i,k}R_{j,k}}{g_k},P(Q,R,g)=Qdiag(g)−1R⊤,Pi,j​=k=1∑r​gk​Qi,k​Rj,k​​,
(42)

where columns with gk=0g_k=0gk​=0 are discarded before applying the formula.

The latent interpretation is immediate. The vector ggg is the law of an intermediate variable Z∈{1,…,r}Z\in\{1,\ldots,r\}Z∈{1,…,r}; QQQ is a coupling of the source index XXX with ZZZ; RRR is a coupling of the target index YYY with the same ZZZ. Formula (42) is the law of (X,Y)(X,Y)(X,Y) obtained by sampling Z∼gZ\sim gZ∼g, then sampling XXX and YYY conditionally independently given ZZZ. Equivalently, OT is replaced by a succession of two transports through an abstract intermediate measure η=∑k=1rgkδzk\eta=\sum_{k=1}^r g_k\delta_{z_k}η=∑k=1r​gk​δzk​​ on an rrr-point space. The locations zkz_kzk​ only label the latent atoms and do not enter the original cost.

Proposition: Factored Couplings and Nonnegative Rank

For every feasible triple (Q,R,g)(Q,R,g)(Q,R,g) in Definition Definition: Low-Rank Factored Couplings, the matrix P(Q,R,g)P(Q,R,g)P(Q,R,g) belongs to U(a,b)\CouplingsD(a,b)U(a,b) and has nonnegative rank at most rrr. Conversely, every coupling P∈U(a,b)P\in\CouplingsD(a,b)P∈U(a,b) with nonnegative rank at most rrr admits a representation of the form (42), after possibly deleting zero latent components.

Proof

The marginal constraints follow by direct summation:

P1m=Qdiag⁡(g)−1R⊤1m=Qdiag⁡(g)−1g=Q1r=a,P\ones_m=Q\operatorname{diag}(g)^{-1}R^\top\ones_m =Q\operatorname{diag}(g)^{-1}g=Q\ones_r=a,P1m​=Qdiag(g)−1R⊤1m​=Qdiag(g)−1g=Q1r​=a,
(43)

and similarly P⊤1n=bP^\top\ones_n=bP⊤1n​=b. Since PPP is a sum of rrr nonnegative rank-one matrices Q:,kR:,k⊤/gkQ_{:,k}R_{:,k}^\top/g_kQ:,k​R:,k⊤​/gk​, its nonnegative rank is at most rrr.

Set qk=∑iUi,kq_k=\sum_i U_{i,k}qk​=∑i​Ui,k​ and sk=∑jVj,ks_k=\sum_j V_{j,k}sk​=∑j​Vj,k​. Components with qksk=0q_ks_k=0qk​sk​=0 do not contribute and can be removed. Define gk=qkskg_k=q_ks_kgk​=qk​sk​, Qi,k=Ui,kskQ_{i,k}=U_{i,k}s_kQi,k​=Ui,k​sk​ and Rj,k=Vj,kqkR_{j,k}=V_{j,k}q_kRj,k​=Vj,k​qk​. Since PPP has total mass one, g∈Δrg\in\simplex_rg∈Δr​. Moreover Q1r=P1m=aQ\ones_r=P\ones_m=aQ1r​=P1m​=a, R1r=P⊤1n=bR\ones_r=P^\top\ones_n=bR1r​=P⊤1n​=b, and both column marginals are equal to ggg. Finally,

∑kQi,kRj,kgk=∑kUi,kskVj,kqkqksk=Pi,j.\sum_k\frac{Q_{i,k}R_{j,k}}{g_k} = \sum_k\frac{U_{i,k}s_kV_{j,k}q_k}{q_ks_k} =P_{i,j}.k∑​gk​Qi,k​Rj,k​​=k∑​qk​sk​Ui,k​sk​Vj,k​qk​​=Pi,j​.

For a cost matrix C∈Rn×mC\in\RR^{n\times m}C∈Rn×m, the low-rank constrained OT value is

min⁡(Q,R,g)∑k=1rQ:,k⊤CR:,kgk.\min_{(Q,R,g)} \sum_{k=1}^r \frac{Q_{:,k}^\top C R_{:,k}}{g_k}.(Q,R,g)min​k=1∑r​gk​Q:,k⊤​CR:,k​​.

The minimization is over triples satisfying Definition Definition: Low-Rank Factored Couplings.

This problem is non-convex, but each factor block has a familiar structure. A common entropic variant adds entropy to the two sub-couplings. In this entropic model one works with positive latent masses gk>0g_k>0gk​>0; components of zero mass are simply removed before solving the problem.

min⁡(Q,R,g)∑k=1rQ:,k⊤CR:,kgk+ϵKL(Q∣a⊗g)+ϵKL(R∣b⊗g),\min_{(Q,R,g)} \sum_{k=1}^r \frac{Q_{:,k}^\top C R_{:,k}}{g_k} + \epsilon\KLD(Q|a\otimes g) + \epsilon\KLD(R|b\otimes g),(Q,R,g)min​k=1∑r​gk​Q:,k⊤​CR:,k​​+ϵKL(Q∣a⊗g)+ϵKL(R∣b⊗g),
(46)

where the constraints are those of Definition Definition: Low-Rank Factored Couplings. The full low-rank Sinkhorn factorization of Scetbon et al. (2021) uses block-coordinate updates in (Q,R,g)(Q,R,g)(Q,R,g). The following fixed-ggg version is the simplest way to see the mechanism: each block update is an ordinary entropic OT problem with an effective cost, and this is the variant used in Figure Div.

Algorithm: Alternating Low-Rank Sinkhorn with Fixed Latent Mass

Input: marginals a∈Δna\in\simplex_na∈Δn​, b∈Δmb\in\simplex_mb∈Δm​, cost C∈Rn×mC\in\RR^{n\times m}C∈Rn×m, rank rrr, positive latent mass g∈Δrg\in\simplex_rg∈Δr​ with gk>0g_k>0gk​>0, regularization ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, maximum number of iterations L≥1L\geq1L≥1, tolerance tol\mathrm{tol}tol.

Output: factored coupling P=Qdiag⁡(g)−1R⊤P=Q\operatorname{diag}(g)^{-1}R^\topP=Qdiag(g)−1R⊤.

Initialize Q(0)=a⊗gQ^{(0)}=a\otimes gQ(0)=a⊗g, R(0)=b⊗gR^{(0)}=b\otimes gR(0)=b⊗g and J(0)=+∞J^{(0)}=+\inftyJ(0)=+∞.

For ℓ=0,…,L−1\ell=0,\ldots,L-1ℓ=0,…,L−1:

  1. Set A(ℓ)=CR(ℓ)diag⁡(g)−1A^{(\ell)}=C R^{(\ell)}\operatorname{diag}(g)^{-1}A(ℓ)=CR(ℓ)diag(g)−1.

  2. Update Q(ℓ+1)Q^{(\ell+1)}Q(ℓ+1) by entropic OT: Q(ℓ+1)=arg⁡min⁡Q1r=a, Q⊤1n=g⟨A(ℓ),Q⟩+ϵKL(Q∣a⊗g)Q^{(\ell+1)}=\arg\min_{Q\ones_r=a,\,Q^\top\ones_n=g} \langle A^{(\ell)},Q\rangle+\epsilon\KLD(Q|a\otimes g)Q(ℓ+1)=argminQ1r​=a,Q⊤1n​=g​⟨A(ℓ),Q⟩+ϵKL(Q∣a⊗g).

  3. Set B(ℓ+1)=C⊤Q(ℓ+1)diag⁡(g)−1B^{(\ell+1)}=C^\top Q^{(\ell+1)}\operatorname{diag}(g)^{-1}B(ℓ+1)=C⊤Q(ℓ+1)diag(g)−1.

  4. Update R(ℓ+1)R^{(\ell+1)}R(ℓ+1) by entropic OT: R(ℓ+1)=arg⁡min⁡R1r=b, R⊤1m=g⟨B(ℓ+1),R⟩+ϵKL(R∣b⊗g)R^{(\ell+1)}=\arg\min_{R\ones_r=b,\,R^\top\ones_m=g} \langle B^{(\ell+1)},R\rangle+\epsilon\KLD(R|b\otimes g)R(ℓ+1)=argminR1r​=b,R⊤1m​=g​⟨B(ℓ+1),R⟩+ϵKL(R∣b⊗g).

  5. Set P(ℓ+1)=Q(ℓ+1)diag⁡(g)−1(R(ℓ+1))⊤P^{(\ell+1)}=Q^{(\ell+1)}\operatorname{diag}(g)^{-1}(R^{(\ell+1)})^\topP(ℓ+1)=Q(ℓ+1)diag(g)−1(R(ℓ+1))⊤.

  6. Set J(ℓ+1)J^{(\ell+1)}J(ℓ+1) to the value of (46) at (Q(ℓ+1),R(ℓ+1),g)(Q^{(\ell+1)},R^{(\ell+1)},g)(Q(ℓ+1),R(ℓ+1),g).

  7. If ℓ≥1\ell\geq1ℓ≥1 and ∣J(ℓ+1)−J(ℓ)∣≤tolmax⁡{1,∣J(ℓ)∣}|J^{(\ell+1)}-J^{(\ell)}|\leq \mathrm{tol}\max\{1,|J^{(\ell)}|\}∣J(ℓ+1)−J(ℓ)∣≤tolmax{1,∣J(ℓ)∣}, return P(ℓ+1)P^{(\ell+1)}P(ℓ+1).

Return P(L)P^{(L)}P(L) if the loop reaches LLL iterations.

show_book_figure("low-rank-ot-factorization")

Low-rank entropic OT on a one-dimensional Gaussian-mixture example. The first view shows factorization through four latent atoms; the matrix panels compare the full entropic coupling with fixed-latent-mass low-rank couplings of increasing rank. This is deliberately not a favorable example for low rank: with a small entropic parameter, one-dimensional quadratic OT is close to a sparse Monge graph rather than to a genuinely low-rank matrix.

Metric Learning and Inverse OT¶

This section points to inverse problems where the ground cost itself is learned. Such problems are typically bilevel and non-convex, but OT provides useful gradients with respect to the cost.

Differentiating OT Losses¶

Inverse OT and metric learning repeatedly differentiate a forward OT value with respect to the input law and to the ground cost. The two resulting objects are precisely the two certificates of optimality: a Kantorovich potential for perturbations of the marginal and an optimal coupling for perturbations of the cost. The main caveat is non-uniqueness. In the unregularized case, the correct objects are one-sided directional derivatives, or equivalently subgradients in the measure variable and supergradients in the cost variable. Entropic regularization selects a unique plan and, for positive finite histograms, gives ordinary derivatives on the simplex interiors.

Proposition: First variations of unregularized OT

Let α∈P(X)\alpha\in\Pp(\Xx)α∈P(X) and β∈P(Y)\beta\in\Pp(\Yy)β∈P(Y), where X,Y\Xx,\YyX,Y are compact metric spaces, and let c∈C(X×Y)c\in\Cc(\Xx\times\Yy)c∈C(X×Y). Define

Vc(α,β):=inf⁡π∈Π(α,β)∫X×Yc(x,y) dπ(x,y).\mathcal V_c(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \inf_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)} \int_{\Xx\times\Yy}c(x,y)\d\pi(x,y).Vc​(α,β):=π∈Π(α,β)inf​∫X×Y​c(x,y)dπ(x,y).

δVcδα=f⋆,δVcδc=π⋆.\frac{\delta \mathcal V_c}{\delta\alpha}=f^\star, \qquad \frac{\delta \mathcal V_c}{\delta c}=\pi^\star .δαδVc​​=f⋆,δcδVc​​=π⋆.

Proof

Kantorovich duality writes

Vc(α,β)=sup⁡f⊕g≤c∫f dα+∫g dβ.\mathcal V_c(\alpha,\beta) = \sup_{f\oplus g\leq c} \int f\d\alpha+\int g\d\beta .Vc​(α,β)=f⊕g≤csup​∫fdα+∫gdβ.
(51)

This is a supremum of affine functions of α\alphaα, so Danskin’s theorem gives the one-sided directional derivative as the supremum over active maximizers, namely the optimal dual potentials. The condition χ(X)=0\chi(\Xx)=0χ(X)=0 makes the formula independent of the additive gauge (f,g)↦(f+λ,g−λ)(f,g)\mapsto(f+\lambda,g-\lambda)(f,g)↦(f+λ,g−λ).

For the cost variable,

Vct(α,β)=inf⁡π∈Π(α,β)∫c dπ+t∫h dπ\mathcal V_{c_t}(\alpha,\beta) = \inf_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)} \int c\d\pi+t\int h\d\piVct​​(α,β)=π∈Π(α,β)inf​∫cdπ+t∫hdπ

is an infimum of affine functions of ttt. Danskin’s theorem for a minimum gives the right directional derivative as the infimum of ∫h dπ\int h\d\pi∫hdπ over the active minimizers. If the active dual potential or coupling is unique, the corresponding directional derivative is linear in the perturbation, which is the displayed first variation.

In the discrete case, this proposition says that any optimal dual vector f⋆f^\starf⋆ is a subgradient with respect to the source weights aaa, while any optimal plan P⋆P^\starP⋆ is a supergradient with respect to the cost matrix CCC, because the value is concave in CCC:

f⋆∈∂aLC(a,b),P⋆∈∂CsupLC(a,b).f^\star\in\partial_a\mathcal L_C(a,b), \qquad P^\star\in\partial_C^{\mathrm{sup}}\mathcal L_C(a,b).f⋆∈∂a​LC​(a,b),P⋆∈∂Csup​LC​(a,b).

Here ∂Csup\partial_C^{\mathrm{sup}}∂Csup​ denotes the superdifferential of the concave map C↦LC(a,b)C\mapsto\mathcal L_C(a,b)C↦LC​(a,b). When the corresponding objects are unique, these inclusions become the gradients ∇aLC(a,b)=f⋆\nabla_a\mathcal L_C(a,b)=f^\star∇a​LC​(a,b)=f⋆ on the tangent space {⟨1,χ⟩=0}\{\dotp{\ones}{\chi}=0\}{⟨1,χ⟩=0} and ∇CLC(a,b)=P⋆\nabla_C\mathcal L_C(a,b)=P^\star∇C​LC​(a,b)=P⋆. Without uniqueness, the exact directional derivative with respect to CCC in a direction ΔC\Delta CΔC is the minimum of ⟨ΔC,P⟩\dotp{\Delta C}{P}⟨ΔC,P⟩ over all optimal plans.

 dπϵ(x,y)=exp⁡ ⁣(fϵ(x)+gϵ(y)−c(x,y)ϵ) dα(x) dβ(y)\d\pi_\epsilon(x,y) = \exp\!\left(\frac{f_\epsilon(x)+g_\epsilon(y)-c(x,y)}{\epsilon}\right) \d\alpha(x)\d\beta(y)dπϵ​(x,y)=exp(ϵfϵ​(x)+gϵ​(y)−c(x,y)​)dα(x)dβ(y)

 d dt∣t=0+Vc,ϵ(αt,β)=∫fϵ dχ, d dt∣t=0+Vct,ϵ(α,β)=∫h dπϵ.\left.\frac{\d}{\d t}\right|_{t=0^+} \mathcal V_{c,\epsilon}(\alpha_t,\beta) = \int f_\epsilon\d\chi, \qquad \left.\frac{\d}{\d t}\right|_{t=0^+} \mathcal V_{c_t,\epsilon}(\alpha,\beta) = \int h\d\pi_\epsilon .dtd​∣∣​t=0+​Vc,ϵ​(αt​,β)=∫fϵ​dχ,dtd​∣∣​t=0+​Vct​,ϵ​(α,β)=∫hdπϵ​.

δVc,ϵδα=fϵ,δVc,ϵδc=πϵ.\frac{\delta \mathcal V_{c,\epsilon}}{\delta\alpha}=f_\epsilon, \qquad \frac{\delta \mathcal V_{c,\epsilon}}{\delta c}=\pi_\epsilon .δαδVc,ϵ​​=fϵ​,δcδVc,ϵ​​=πϵ​.

The cost derivative follows directly from the primal envelope theorem, because the entropic optimizer is unique. For the measure derivative, use the continuous entropic dual formula from the Sinkhorn chapter. At an optimal pair, the soft-transform equations imply the row normalization

∫Yexp⁡ ⁣(fϵ(x)+gϵ(y)−c(x,y)ϵ) dβ(y)=1for all x.\int_{\Yy} \exp\!\left(\frac{f_\epsilon(x)+g_\epsilon(y)-c(x,y)}{\epsilon}\right) \d\beta(y) =1 \qquad\text{for all }x.∫Y​exp(ϵfϵ​(x)+gϵ​(y)−c(x,y)​)dβ(y)=1for all x.

For a finite-dimensional parametrization cθc_\thetacθ​ or CθC_\thetaCθ​, the entropic formula gives the backpropagation rule

LCϵ(a,b)=VC,ϵ(a,b)−ϵH(a)−ϵH(b),\mathcal L_C^\epsilon(a,b) = \mathcal V_{C,\epsilon}(a,b) - \epsilon H(a)-\epsilon H(b),LCϵ​(a,b)=VC,ϵ​(a,b)−ϵH(a)−ϵH(b),

Inverse Optimal Transport¶

Inverse OT asks for a ground cost that explains observed matchings or flows as optimal transport plans. In its most direct form, one observes a plan π^\widehat\piπ with marginals (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)(α,β) and seeks a cost ccc such that π^\widehat\piπ is optimal for

inf⁡π∈Π(α,β)∫c(x,y) dπ(x,y).\inf_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)} \int c(x,y)\d\pi(x,y).π∈Π(α,β)inf​∫c(x,y)dπ(x,y).
(62)

This is ill-posed without structure: adding potentials u(x)+v(y)u(x)+v(y)u(x)+v(y) to a cost does not change the set of optimal couplings, and many costs can rationalize the same sparse plan.

A useful statistical methodology is to measure the suboptimality of the observed plan through a Fenchel--Young loss. Write the score as s=−cs=-cs=−c and define the convex regularized prediction value

Gϵ(s)=sup⁡π∈Π(α,β)∫s dπ−ϵKL⁡(π∣α⊗β).G_\epsilon(s) = \sup_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)} \int s\d\pi - \epsilon\operatorname{KL}(\pi\mid\alpha\otimes\beta).Gϵ​(s)=π∈Π(α,β)sup​∫sdπ−ϵKL(π∣α⊗β).
(63)

The Fenchel--Young loss

Lϵ(c;π^)=Gϵ(−c)+Gϵ∗(π^)+∫c dπ^\mathcal L_\epsilon(c;\widehat\pi) = G_\epsilon(-c) + G_\epsilon^*(\widehat\pi) + \int c\d\widehat\piLϵ​(c;π)=Gϵ​(−c)+Gϵ∗​(π)+∫cdπ
(64)

is nonnegative by Fenchel’s inequality and vanishes exactly when π^∈∂Gϵ(−c)\widehat\pi\in\partial G_\epsilon(-c)π∈∂Gϵ​(−c), i.e. when π^\widehat\piπ satisfies the regularized optimality conditions for ccc. Entropic regularization is important here because it makes the forward map smoother and provides gradients with respect to ccc, at the price of a statistical bias Andrade et al., 2025Peyré et al., 2026.

In the discrete unregularized case, this loss reduces to the optimality gap of the observed coupling. For P^∈U(a,b)\widehat P\in\mathbf U(a,b)P∈U(a,b) and a cost matrix CCC, denote it by

LiOT(C;P^)=⟨C,P^⟩−min⁡P∈U(a,b)⟨C,P⟩.\mathcal L_{\mathrm{iOT}}(C;\widehat P) = \dotp{C}{\widehat P} - \min_{P\in\mathbf U(a,b)}\dotp{C}{P}.LiOT​(C;P)=⟨C,P⟩−P∈U(a,b)min​⟨C,P⟩.
(65)

This inverse-OT gap loss is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when P^\widehat PP is optimal for CCC.

In practice, one restricts the cost to a finite-dimensional model class, often affine:

Cθ=∑r=1RθrC(r),θ∈Θ,C_\theta=\sum_{r=1}^R\theta_r C^{(r)}, \qquad \theta\in\Theta,Cθ​=r=1∑R​θr​C(r),θ∈Θ,
(66)

where Θ\ThetaΘ is convex and the matrices C(r)C^{(r)}C(r) encode features, graph distances or a Mahalanobis parameterization. This viewpoint appears in low-rank and sparse inverse OT models Dupuy et al., 2019Andrade et al., 2024 and in convex formulations for learning OT costs from observed plans Ma et al., 2020Peyré et al., 2026.

A minimal finite-dimensional model is obtained by learning a bilinear cost on Rd\RR^dRd,

cA(x,y)=⟨Ax,y⟩,A∈Rd×d.c_A(x,y)=\dotp{Ax}{y}, \qquad A\in\RR^{d\times d}.cA​(x,y)=⟨Ax,y⟩,A∈Rd×d.
(67)

For empirical measures α=1n∑iδxi\alpha=\frac1n\sum_i\delta_{x_i}α=n1​∑i​δxi​​ and β=1n∑jδyj\beta=\frac1n\sum_j\delta_{y_j}β=n1​∑j​δyj​​, this gives the cost matrix

C(A)i,j=⟨Axi,yj⟩,C(A)_{i,j}=\dotp{Ax_i}{y_j},C(A)i,j​=⟨Axi​,yj​⟩,
(68)

so both maps A↦C(A)A\mapsto C(A)A↦C(A) and A↦cAA\mapsto c_AA↦cA​ are linear. Inverse OT within this model asks which matrix AAA makes an observed matching or coupling look optimal; learning the cost is thus reduced to estimating a linear parameter.

For a fixed matrix AAA, the forward prediction is the optimal face

PA:=arg min⁡P∈U(1n/n,1n/n)⟨C(A),P⟩.\mathcal P_A\eqdef \uargmin{P\in\CouplingsD(\ones_n/n,\ones_n/n)} \dotp{C(A)}{P}.PA​:=P∈U(1n​/n,1n​/n)argmin​⟨C(A),P⟩.
(69)

When this face is a singleton, write its element as PAP_APA​; otherwise PAP_APA​ denotes a deterministic tie-broken selection. Although A↦C(A)A\mapsto C(A)A↦C(A) is linear, the solution correspondence A↦PAA\mapsto\mathcal P_AA↦PA​ is polyhedral: changing AAA changes the direction in which the transport polytope is probed, and a tie-broken selection is constant on normal-cone cells. The figure below illustrates this correspondence on the OT4ML point clouds. The construction follows the visual idea of the Python Optimal Transport logo Flamary et al., 2021: red source atoms, blue target atoms and straight segments show the selected optimal bijection. With e=(1,1)⊤e=(1,1)^\tope=(1,1)⊤ and δ=10−3\delta=10^{-3}δ=10−3, the first two rank-one matrices are

Ah=−e1e⊤+δe2e⊤,Av=δe1e⊤−e2e⊤.A_h=-e_1e^\top+\delta e_2e^\top, \qquad A_v=\delta e_1e^\top-e_2e^\top .Ah​=−e1​e⊤+δe2​e⊤,Av​=δe1​e⊤−e2​e⊤.
(70)

These small transverse terms break the large ties of the pure horizontal or vertical scores while preserving a rank-one cost. The matrix A=−IA=-IA=−I gives the usual quadratic W2\Wass_2W2​ assignment, up to the marginal-only terms discussed below, while A=+IA=+IA=+I reverses the correlation and produces an anti-W2\Wass_2W2​ matching.

show_book_figure("inverse-ot-bilinear-logo-map")

Forward solutions of the bilinear cost cA(x,y)=⟨Ax,y⟩c_A(x,y)=\dotp{Ax}{y}cA​(x,y)=⟨Ax,y⟩ on the OT4ML logo point clouds. Each panel solves the equal-weight assignment problem with a different matrix AAA; the first two use δ=10−3\delta=10^{-3}δ=10−3 to break rank-one ties. The source atoms are red, the target atoms are blue, and the gray segments give one deterministic optimal bijection.

This elementary model already contains the quadratic Wasserstein assignment. Adding to a cost matrix a term depending only on xix_ixi​ or only on yjy_jyj​ shifts all feasible couplings by the same constant, and therefore does not change the optimizer. Since

∥x−y∥2=∥x∥2+∥y∥2−2⟨x,y⟩,\norm{x-y}^2=\norm{x}^2+\norm{y}^2-2\dotp{x}{y},∥x−y∥2=∥x∥2+∥y∥2−2⟨x,y⟩,
(71)

the usual quadratic Wasserstein assignment has the same optimizer as the bilinear cost with A⋆=−IA_\star=-IA⋆​=−I, up to these marginal-only terms and an irrelevant positive factor. The inverse problem goes in the opposite direction: after observing a coupling, one asks which matrices AAA could have generated it. The next figure generates an observed coupling P^\widehat PP from this cost on two empirical mixtures of Gaussians, and then evaluates LiOT(C(At);P^)\mathcal L_{\mathrm{iOT}}(C(A_t);\widehat P)LiOT​(C(At​);P) along the anisotropic path

At=−diag⁡(1+t,1−t),−1≤t≤1,A_t=-\diag(1+t,1-t), \qquad -1\leq t\leq 1,At​=−diag(1+t,1−t),−1≤t≤1,
(72)

so that t=0t=0t=0 recovers the matrix that generated the observed coupling. Equivalently, with equal weights, P^∈U(1n/n,1n/n)=Bn/n\widehat P\in\CouplingsD(\ones_n/n,\ones_n/n)=\mathcal B_n/nP∈U(1n​/n,1n​/n)=Bn​/n, and the plotted loss is the Kantorovich gap

LiOT(C(At);P^)=⟨C(At),P^⟩−min⁡P∈U(1n/n,1n/n)⟨C(At),P⟩,C(At)i,j=⟨Atxi,yj⟩.\mathcal L_{\mathrm{iOT}}(C(A_t);\widehat P) = \dotp{C(A_t)}{\widehat P} - \min_{P\in\CouplingsD(\ones_n/n,\ones_n/n)} \dotp{C(A_t)}{P}, \qquad C(A_t)_{i,j}=\dotp{A_t x_i}{y_j}.LiOT​(C(At​);P)=⟨C(At​),P⟩−P∈U(1n​/n,1n​/n)min​⟨C(At​),P⟩,C(At​)i,j​=⟨At​xi​,yj​⟩.
(73)

Because t↦C(At)t\mapsto C(A_t)t↦C(At​) is affine and the Kantorovich value is a minimum of affine functions over the fixed polytope U(1n/n,1n/n)\CouplingsD(\ones_n/n,\ones_n/n)U(1n​/n,1n​/n), this one-dimensional gap is convex and piecewise affine. Its zero set can contain an interval for a small sample, reflecting the fact that the same observed coupling remains optimal for a cone of nearby costs.

show_book_figure("inverse-ot-gap-loss")

Inverse-OT gap loss for a bilinear cost. Panel (a): two empirical mixtures of two Gaussians are matched with the cost cA⋆(x,y)=⟨A⋆x,y⟩c_{A_\star}(x,y)=\dotp{A_\star x}{y}cA⋆​​(x,y)=⟨A⋆​x,y⟩ for A⋆=−IA_\star=-IA⋆​=−I, which gives the same optimizer as the quadratic W2\Wass_2W2​ cost; red and blue level sets display the two sampling densities. Panels (b,c): the unregularized Fenchel--Young Kantorovich gap LiOT(C(At);P^)\mathcal L_{\mathrm{iOT}}(C(A_t);\widehat P)LiOT​(C(At​);P) along At=−diag⁡(1+t,1−t)A_t=-\diag(1+t,1-t)At​=−diag(1+t,1−t) for n=10n=10n=10 and n=100n=100n=100, using the same vertical scale. The red dot marks the generating parameter t=0t=0t=0; the curves are convex and piecewise affine.

The comparison between n=10n=10n=10 and n=100n=100n=100 illustrates an important statistical effect: as the number of sampled points grows, the flat region of the empirical gap typically shrinks and the loss develops more visible curvature around the generating parameter. This anticipates the population theory of Peyré, Poon and Tron Peyré et al., 2026: in the limit n→+∞n\to+\inftyn→+∞, when the limiting Monge map itself has nondegenerate curvature as the cost parameter varies, the iOT loss identifies the cost robustly, up to the usual marginal-only gauge freedoms. In that regime, minimizing the gap is not only a certificate of optimality of the observed transport, but also a stable way to recover the underlying cost.

Proposition: Convex Dual-Gap Formulation of Inverse OT

Let P^∈U(a,b)\widehat P\in\mathbf U(a,b)P∈U(a,b) be an observed coupling and let CθC_\thetaCθ​ depend affinely on θ∈Θ\theta\in\Thetaθ∈Θ, where Θ\ThetaΘ is convex. The condition that P^\widehat PP is optimal for the cost CθC_\thetaCθ​ is equivalent to the existence of dual potentials (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) such that

fi+gj≤(Cθ)i,jand∑i,jP^i,j((Cθ)i,j−fi−gj)=0.f_i+g_j\leq (C_\theta)_{i,j} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sum_{i,j}\widehat P_{i,j} \big((C_\theta)_{i,j}-f_i-g_j\big)=0.fi​+gj​≤(Cθ​)i,j​andi,j∑​Pi,j​((Cθ​)i,j​−fi​−gj​)=0.
(74)

Consequently, for a convex regularizer RRR, the noisy inverse problem can be relaxed as the convex program

min⁡θ∈Θ,f,gR(θ)+λ∑i,jP^i,j((Cθ)i,j−fi−gj)\min_{\theta\in\Theta,f,g} R(\theta) + \lambda \sum_{i,j}\widehat P_{i,j} \big((C_\theta)_{i,j}-f_i-g_j\big)θ∈Θ,f,gmin​R(θ)+λi,j∑​Pi,j​((Cθ​)i,j​−fi​−gj​)
(75)

subject to fi+gj≤(Cθ)i,jf_i+g_j\leq(C_\theta)_{i,j}fi​+gj​≤(Cθ​)i,j​ for all i,ji,ji,j.

Proof

For a fixed cost CθC_\thetaCθ​, Kantorovich duality gives

min⁡P∈U(a,b)⟨Cθ,P⟩=max⁡fi+gj≤(Cθ)i,j⟨f,a⟩+⟨g,b⟩.\min_{P\in\mathbf U(a,b)} \dotp{C_\theta}{P} = \max_{f_i+g_j\leq(C_\theta)_{i,j}} \dotp{f}{a}+\dotp{g}{b}.P∈U(a,b)min​⟨Cθ​,P⟩=fi​+gj​≤(Cθ​)i,j​max​⟨f,a⟩+⟨g,b⟩.
(76)

Since P^\widehat PP has marginals (a,b)(a,b)(a,b), every dual feasible pair satisfies

⟨Cθ,P^⟩−⟨f,a⟩−⟨g,b⟩=∑i,jP^i,j((Cθ)i,j−fi−gj)≥0.\dotp{C_\theta}{\widehat P} - \dotp{f}{a} - \dotp{g}{b} = \sum_{i,j}\widehat P_{i,j} \big((C_\theta)_{i,j}-f_i-g_j\big) \geq0.⟨Cθ​,P⟩−⟨f,a⟩−⟨g,b⟩=i,j∑​Pi,j​((Cθ​)i,j​−fi​−gj​)≥0.
(77)

This nonnegative quantity is exactly the primal-dual gap of P^\widehat PP. It vanishes if and only if P^\widehat PP reaches the dual value and is therefore optimal. If CθC_\thetaCθ​ is affine and Θ\ThetaΘ and RRR are convex, the constraints and objective in (75) are convex.

The formulation is useful because it avoids differentiating through a forward OT solver: it learns a cost by making the observed plan satisfy complementary slackness. In statistical settings, P^\widehat PP is only partially observed or noisy, so one adds sparsity, low-rank, smoothness or metric constraints to select a meaningful cost. For entropic OT, the optimality condition becomes smoother:

P^i,j≈aibjexp⁡ ⁣(fi+gj−(Cθ)i,jϵ),\widehat P_{i,j} \approx a_i b_j \exp\!\left( \frac{f_i+g_j-(C_\theta)_{i,j}}{\epsilon} \right),Pi,j​≈ai​bj​exp(ϵfi​+gj​−(Cθ​)i,j​​),
(78)

which leads to likelihood-based or KL-based convex objectives when CθC_\thetaCθ​ is affine, and connects inverse OT with generalized Sinkhorn iterations and transport-regularized inverse problems Karlsson & Ringh, 2016Ma et al., 2020.

Algorithm: Inverse OT by dual-gap fitting

Input: Observed plan P^∈U(a,b)\widehat P\in\CouplingsD(\a,\b)P∈U(a,b), features C(r)C^{(r)}C(r), feasible set Θ\ThetaΘ, regularizer RRR.

Output: Identified cost Cθ⋆C_{\theta^\star}Cθ⋆​ and potentials (f⋆,g⋆)(f^\star,g^\star)(f⋆,g⋆).

Set parametric cost: Cθ=∑rθrC(r).C_\theta=\sum_r\theta_r C^{(r)}.Cθ​=∑r​θr​C(r).

Let (θ⋆,f⋆,g⋆)(\theta^\star,f^\star,g^\star)(θ⋆,f⋆,g⋆) be a minimizer of min⁡θ∈Θ,f,gR(θ)+λ∑i,jP^i,j((Cθ)i,j−fi−gj)\min_{\theta\in\Theta,f,g} R(\theta)+\lambda \sum_{i,j}\widehat P_{i,j}\big((C_\theta)_{i,j}-f_i-g_j\big)minθ∈Θ,f,g​R(θ)+λ∑i,j​Pi,j​((Cθ​)i,j​−fi​−gj​)

Subject to fi+gj≤(Cθ)i,jfor all (i,j).f_i+g_j\leq(C_\theta)_{i,j} \qquad\text{for all }(i,j).fi​+gj​≤(Cθ​)i,j​for all (i,j). Return θ⋆\theta^\starθ⋆, Cθ⋆C_{\theta^\star}Cθ⋆​, and (f⋆,g⋆)(f^\star,g^\star)(f⋆,g⋆).

Weak Optimal Transport¶

Weak OT relaxes the cost so that it depends on the conditional distribution of destinations rather than only on pointwise pairs. It is useful when a source point is allowed to choose a randomized response and the model only penalizes an aggregate of that response, such as its conditional mean.

Barycentric Projection of a Coupling¶

The first object to isolate is the map obtained by collapsing each conditional law to its barycenter.

Definition: Barycentric Projection of a Coupling

Let α,β∈P1(Rd)\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal P_1(\RR^d)α,β∈P1​(Rd) and let π∈Π(α,β)\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)π∈Π(α,β). Disintegrate π\piπ with respect to its first marginal as π( dx, dy)=πx( dy)α( dx)\pi(\d x,\d y)=\pi_x(\d y)\alpha(\d x)π(dx,dy)=πx​(dy)α(dx). Since β\betaβ has finite first moment, the conditional mean is finite for α\alphaα-a.e. xxx, and the barycentric projection of π\piπ is the map

Tˉπ(x):=∫Rdy dπx(y),βˉπ:=(Tˉπ)♯α.\bar T_\pi(x) \eqdef \int_{\RR^d}y\d\pi_x(y), \qquad \bar\beta_\pi \eqdef (\bar T_\pi)_\sharp\alpha.Tˉπ​(x):=∫Rd​ydπx​(y),βˉ​π​:=(Tˉπ​)♯​α.
(79)

The projected target βˉπ\bar\beta_\piβˉ​π​ records the distribution of conditional means, not the full second marginal. Thus it is generally different from β\betaβ; if π=(Id,T)♯α\pi=(\Id,T)_\sharp\alphaπ=(Id,T)♯​α is induced by a map, then Tˉπ=T\bar T_\pi=TTˉπ​=T and βˉπ=β\bar\beta_\pi=\betaβˉ​π​=β. This projection is not an optimal map for an arbitrary coupling: a deterministic rotation of a radially symmetric source, for example, projects to the rotation itself, whereas the optimal map from the source to itself is the identity. The useful positive statement is attached to quadratic optimal plans, as in the tangent-space viewpoint on W2\Wass_2W2​ developed by Ambrosio, Gigli and Savare Ambrosio et al., 2006.

Proposition: Barycentric Projection of a Quadratic Optimal Plan

Let π∈Π(α,β)\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)π∈Π(α,β) be optimal for the quadratic cost ∥x−y∥2\norm{x-y}^2∥x−y∥2 between α,β∈P2(Rd)\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal P_2(\RR^d)α,β∈P2​(Rd), and define Tˉπ\bar T_\piTˉπ​ and βˉπ\bar\beta_\piβˉ​π​ by (79). Then (Id,Tˉπ)♯α(\Id,\bar T_\pi)_\sharp\alpha(Id,Tˉπ​)♯​α is an optimal coupling between α\alphaα and βˉπ\bar\beta_\piβˉ​π​. Equivalently, Tˉπ\bar T_\piTˉπ​ is a quadratic optimal transport map from α\alphaα to the projected target βˉπ\bar\beta_\piβˉ​π​.

Proof

By the cyclic-monotonicity characterization of quadratic optimality, π\piπ is concentrated on a ccc-cyclically monotone set Γ\GammaΓ for c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2c(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^2c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2. This means that every finite cycle (xi,yi)i=1m⊂Γ(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^m\subset\Gamma(xi​,yi​)i=1m​⊂Γ satisfies

∑i=1m⟨xi,yi⟩≥∑i=1m⟨xi,yi+1⟩,ym+1=y1.\sum_{i=1}^m\dotp{x_i}{y_i} \geq \sum_{i=1}^m\dotp{x_i}{y_{i+1}}, \qquad y_{m+1}=y_1.i=1∑m​⟨xi​,yi​⟩≥i=1∑m​⟨xi​,yi+1​⟩,ym+1​=y1​.
(80)

After changing the disintegration on an α\alphaα-negligible set, πx\pi_xπx​ is supported on the section Γx={y:(x,y)∈Γ}\Gamma_x=\{y:(x,y)\in\Gamma\}Γx​={y:(x,y)∈Γ} for α\alphaα-almost every xxx. Choose x1,…,xmx_1,\ldots,x_mx1​,…,xm​ in this full-measure set and independently sample Yi∼πxiY_i\sim\pi_{x_i}Yi​∼πxi​​. Applying the cyclic inequality to (xi,Yi)(x_i,Y_i)(xi​,Yi​) and taking expectations gives

∑i=1m⟨xi,Tˉπ(xi)⟩≥∑i=1m⟨xi,Tˉπ(xi+1)⟩.\sum_{i=1}^m\dotp{x_i}{\bar T_\pi(x_i)} \geq \sum_{i=1}^m\dotp{x_i}{\bar T_\pi(x_{i+1})}.i=1∑m​⟨xi​,Tˉπ​(xi​)⟩≥i=1∑m​⟨xi​,Tˉπ​(xi+1​)⟩.
(81)

Thus (Id,Tˉπ)♯α(\Id,\bar T_\pi)_\sharp\alpha(Id,Tˉπ​)♯​α is concentrated on a cyclically monotone graph. By the cyclic-monotonicity characterization of quadratic optimality, this plan is optimal between its two marginals.

Weak transport costs use the same disintegration but allow the objective to depend on the whole conditional law, or on summaries such as the barycentric projection (79). The framework was introduced through general transport costs and weak transport inequalities, with existence, duality and optimality conditions developed on Polish spaces Gozlan et al., 2017Backhoff Veraguas et al., 2018. For a weak cost C:X×P(Y)→R∪{+∞}C:\X\times\mathcal P(\Y)\to\RR\cup\{+\infty\}C:X×P(Y)→R∪{+∞}, the weak OT value is

WC(α,β):=inf⁡π∈Π(α,β)∫C(x,πx) dα(x).\mathcal W_C(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \inf_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)} \int C(x,\pi_x)\d\alpha(x).WC​(α,β):=π∈Π(α,β)inf​∫C(x,πx​)dα(x).
(82)

The classical Kantorovich problem is recovered when C(x,ν)=∫c(x,y) dν(y)C(x,\nu)=\int c(x,y)\d\nu(y)C(x,ν)=∫c(x,y)dν(y), because the objective then becomes ∫c(x,y) dπ(x,y)\int c(x,y)\d\pi(x,y)∫c(x,y)dπ(x,y). The genuinely weak behavior starts when CCC is nonlinear in ν\nuν.

Proposition: Weak Kantorovich Duality

Assume that X,Y\X,\YX,Y are compact metric spaces and that C(x,ν)C(x,\nu)C(x,ν) is lower semicontinuous, bounded from below and convex in ν\nuν, with the standard qualification assumptions ensuring Fenchel--Rockafellar duality. For g∈C(Y)g\in\mathcal C(\Y)g∈C(Y) define the weak CCC-transform

gC(x):=inf⁡ν∈P(Y){C(x,ν)−∫g(y) dν(y)}.g^C(x) \eqdef \inf_{\nu\in\mathcal P(\Y)} \left\{ C(x,\nu)-\int g(y)\d\nu(y) \right\}.gC(x):=ν∈P(Y)inf​{C(x,ν)−∫g(y)dν(y)}.
(83)

Then

WC(α,β)=sup⁡g∈C(Y){∫gC(x) dα(x)+∫g(y) dβ(y)}.\mathcal W_C(\alpha,\beta) = \sup_{g\in\mathcal C(\Y)} \left\{ \int g^C(x)\d\alpha(x) + \int g(y)\d\beta(y) \right\}.WC​(α,β)=g∈C(Y)sup​{∫gC(x)dα(x)+∫g(y)dβ(y)}.
(84)

When C(x,ν)=∫c(x,y) dν(y)C(x,\nu)=\int c(x,y)\d\nu(y)C(x,ν)=∫c(x,y)dν(y), this reduces to the usual Kantorovich dual with gC(x)=inf⁡y(c(x,y)−g(y))g^C(x)=\inf_y(c(x,y)-g(y))gC(x)=infy​(c(x,y)−g(y)).

Proof

For any coupling π\piπ and any g∈C(Y)g\in\mathcal C(\Y)g∈C(Y), the definition of gCg^CgC gives

C(x,πx)≥gC(x)+∫g(y) dπx(y).C(x,\pi_x) \geq g^C(x) + \int g(y)\d\pi_x(y).C(x,πx​)≥gC(x)+∫g(y)dπx​(y).
(85)

After integration with respect to α\alphaα, the second term becomes ∫g dβ\int g\d\beta∫gdβ because the second marginal of π\piπ is β\betaβ. This proves weak duality.

For the reverse inequality, consider the convex minimization over probability kernels x↦πxx\mapsto\pi_xx↦πx​ with the affine constraint ∫πx dα(x)=β\int \pi_x\d\alpha(x)=\beta∫πx​dα(x)=β. Fenchel--Rockafellar duality gives a continuous Lagrange multiplier ggg for this marginal constraint. Minimizing the Lagrangian over each conditional law gives exactly the pointwise term gC(x)g^C(x)gC(x), while the multiplier contributes ∫g dβ\int g\d\beta∫gdβ. The compactness, lower semicontinuity, convexity and qualification assumptions ensure no duality gap.

Proposition: Barycentric Weak Transport Is Weaker than W2\Wass_2W2​

Let α,β∈P2(Rd)\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal P_2(\RR^d)α,β∈P2​(Rd) and define

Cbar(x,ν)=∥x−∫y dν(y)∥2.C_{\mathrm{bar}}(x,\nu) = \norm{x-\int y\d\nu(y)}^2.Cbar​(x,ν)=∥∥​x−∫ydν(y)∥∥​2.
(86)

Equivalently, for a coupling π\piπ, the integrand is ∥x−Tˉπ(x)∥2\norm{x-\bar T_\pi(x)}^2∥∥​x−Tˉπ​(x)∥∥​2. Then

WCbar(α,β)≤W22(α,β).\mathcal W_{C_{\mathrm{bar}}}(\alpha,\beta) \leq \Wass_2^2(\alpha,\beta).WCbar​​(α,β)≤W22​(α,β).
(87)
Proof

Let π\piπ be any coupling and disintegrate it as πxα\pi_x\alphaπx​α. By Jensen’s inequality,

∥x−Tˉπ(x)∥2≤∫∥x−y∥2 dπx(y).\norm{x-\bar T_\pi(x)}^2 \leq \int\norm{x-y}^2\d\pi_x(y).∥∥​x−Tˉπ​(x)∥∥​2≤∫∥x−y∥2dπx​(y).
(88)

Integrating in xxx gives ∫Cbar(x,πx) dα(x)≤∫∥x−y∥2 dπ(x,y)\int C_{\mathrm{bar}}(x,\pi_x)\d\alpha(x)\leq \int\norm{x-y}^2\d\pi(x,y)∫Cbar​(x,πx​)dα(x)≤∫∥x−y∥2dπ(x,y). Taking the infimum over π\piπ proves the claim.

show_book_figure("weak-ot-barycentric-projection")

Weak barycentric transport on a small disk-to-annulus coupling. The left panel shows the full conditional laws: each red source atom splits its mass among several blue target atoms, with segment thickness proportional to transported mass. The right panel collapses each conditional law πx\pi_xπx​ to its barycenter Tˉπ(x)=∫y dπx(y)\bar T_\pi(x)=\int y\d\pi_x(y)Tˉπ​(x)=∫ydπx​(y), shown in violet. The barycentric weak cost only sees the red-to-violet displacement, and therefore ignores the conditional spread around each barycenter.

The interactive demo lets each source point split toward several targets. Increasing the split count or spread usually increases the full quadratic cost while the weak barycentric cost can remain much smaller.

Interactive panel. Use the spread and barycentric controls to compare full weak conditional laws with their barycentric projections.

The barycentric cost is the canonical example to keep in mind: admissibility still constrains the full conditional laws to have second marginal β\betaβ, but the objective only charges the displacement from xxx to Tˉπ(x)\bar T_\pi(x)Tˉπ​(x) and ignores the conditional variance around this barycenter. This connects weak OT with martingale transport, Strassen-type convex-order constraints, barycentric projections and learning problems where conditional averages are meaningful objects.

Martingale Optimal Transport¶

Martingale OT is the extreme barycentric version of the weak viewpoint: a source point may split randomly, but the average destination must remain equal to the source point. This turns the barycentric projection from an object used in the cost into a hard constraint.

Definition: Martingale Couplings and Martingale OT

Let α,β∈P1(Rd)\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal P_1(\RR^d)α,β∈P1​(Rd). A coupling π∈Π(α,β)\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)π∈Π(α,β) is a martingale coupling if, for the disintegration π( dx, dy)=πx( dy)α( dx)\pi(\d x,\d y)=\pi_x(\d y)\alpha(\d x)π(dx,dy)=πx​(dy)α(dx),

∫Rdy dπx(y)=xfor α-a.e. x.\int_{\RR^d}y\d\pi_x(y)=x \qquad\text{for $\alpha$-a.e. }x .∫Rd​ydπx​(y)=xfor α-a.e. x.
(89)

Equivalently, Tˉπ=Id\bar T_\pi=\IdTˉπ​=Id in (79). The set of such couplings is

Πmart(α,β):={π∈Π(α,β)  :  Tˉπ=Idα-a.e.}.\Couplings_{\mathrm{mart}}(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \left\{ \pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)\;:\; \bar T_\pi=\Id\quad\alpha\text{-a.e.} \right\}.Πmart​(α,β):={π∈Π(α,β):Tˉπ​=Idα-a.e.}.
(90)

For a cost ccc, the martingale OT value is +∞+\infty+∞ if the admissible set is empty, and otherwise is obtained by minimizing ∫c dπ\int c\d\pi∫cdπ over Πmart(α,β)\Couplings_{\mathrm{mart}}(\alpha,\beta)Πmart​(α,β).

The terminology comes from probability: if (X,Y)∼π(X,Y)\sim\pi(X,Y)∼π, then (89) is exactly E[Y∣X]=X\mathbb E[Y|X]=XE[Y∣X]=X. Hence martingale OT is a Kantorovich problem with the usual two marginal constraints plus a barycentric constraint on the conditional laws. Equivalently, the barycentric projected coupling (Id,Tˉπ)♯α(\Id,\bar T_\pi)_\sharp\alpha(Id,Tˉπ​)♯​α must be the diagonal coupling (Id,Id)♯α(\Id,\Id)_\sharp\alpha(Id,Id)♯​α. This is stronger than merely asking the projected target (Tˉπ)♯α(\bar T_\pi)_\sharp\alpha(Tˉπ​)♯​α to equal α\alphaα, since a nontrivial measure-preserving map could have the same projected marginal without satisfying Tˉπ(x)=x\bar T_\pi(x)=xTˉπ​(x)=x pointwise. Martingale OT is central in robust finance, where one transports today prices to tomorrow prices without introducing drift, and has led to a rich martingale transport theory Beiglböck et al., 2013Galichon et al., 2014Dolinsky & Soner, 2014Guo & Obloj, 2017.

Stochastic Orders¶

The admissibility of martingale couplings is governed by stochastic order. For measures on R\RRR, the classical stochastic order is

α⪯stβ⟺∫φ  dα≤∫φ  dβfor every increasing φ.\alpha\preceq_{\mathrm{st}}\beta \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \int\varphi\,\d\alpha\leq\int\varphi\,\d\beta \quad\text{for every increasing }\varphi .α⪯st​β⟺∫φdα≤∫φdβfor every increasing φ.
(91)

Strassen’s theorem Strassen, 1965 says that this is equivalent to the existence of a coupling (X,Y)(X,Y)(X,Y) with X≤YX\leq YX≤Y almost surely. Thus an order inequality between laws is represented by a pathwise constraint on a coupling.

For martingale OT the relevant order is the convex order. For measures with finite first moments,

α⪯cxβ⟺∫φ  dα≤∫φ  dβfor every convex φ with finite integrals.\alpha\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}\beta \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \int\varphi\,\d\alpha\leq\int\varphi\,\d\beta \quad\text{for every convex }\varphi\text{ with finite integrals}.α⪯cx​β⟺∫φdα≤∫φdβfor every convex φ with finite integrals.
(92)

Testing affine functions gives equality of means, while convex test functions say that β\betaβ is more spread out than α\alphaα. For Gaussian measures with the same mean, this reduces to the Loewner order on covariance matrices:

N(m,Σ0)⪯cxN(m,Σ1)⟺Σ1−Σ0⪰0.\mathcal N(m,\Sigma_0)\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}\mathcal N(m,\Sigma_1) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Sigma_1-\Sigma_0\succeq0 .N(m,Σ0​)⪯cx​N(m,Σ1​)⟺Σ1​−Σ0​⪰0.
(93)

Indeed, if Σ1−Σ0⪰0\Sigma_1-\Sigma_0\succeq0Σ1​−Σ0​⪰0, then N(m,Σ1)\mathcal N(m,\Sigma_1)N(m,Σ1​) is obtained from N(m,Σ0)\mathcal N(m,\Sigma_0)N(m,Σ0​) by adding independent centered Gaussian noise. Conversely, testing the convex quadratic functions x↦⟨u,x⟩2x\mapsto\langle u,x\rangle^2x↦⟨u,x⟩2 gives the Loewner inequality.

Strassen’s martingale theorem states that α⪯cxβ\alpha\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}\betaα⪯cx​β if and only if Πmart(α,β)\Couplings_{\mathrm{mart}}(\alpha,\beta)Πmart​(α,β) is nonempty. Hence convex order is exactly the feasibility condition for martingale OT.
